name: recv-table

name: merge-before-opcode
bug: reads ar$op before touching the table and learns only from a REPLY, treating a REQUEST as a question to answer rather than information to merge; this is the error RFC 826 shouts at in the only double exclamation in the document, line 219 '(NOW look at the opcode!!)', and spends lines 227-229 restating. THE MANDATORY FAMOUS-BUG MUTANT
shape: opcode independence of the table outcome, stated by enumerating the two Opcode values in the post; op is a parameter of the contract and absent from the body
mutant_verdict: refuted: recv-merge (else-branch does not satisfy postcondition, constraint #3)
refuted_by: [A61] the REQUEST arm and the REPLY arm of the table outcome disagree

name: recv-reply

shape: emitted packet as a CONSTRUCTED n-arm sum with a nested-pair payload ((ar$sha, ar$spa), (ar$tha, ar$tpa)) plus destination; NoEmission as a real value for the discard rule; a separate ReplyBroadcast arm so the destination mode S5 of line 224 is expressible at all

name: resolve-out
bug: fills ar$spa with the target protocol address instead of its own, transposing the two adjacent 'of itself' / 'of the machine that is trying to be accessed' assignments of lines 181-184; the broadcast request then announces <target protocol address, requester hardware address>, which every station holding an entry for the target merges unconditionally under lines 210-213, blackholing the machine the requester was trying to reach on the whole cable at once
shape: outbound half as one total function over hit and miss; opcode and destination mode carried by the constructor (BroadcastRequest has no REPLY inhabitant, so A37 and A43 discharge by construction); ar$tha deliberately absent per lines 184-185
mutant_verdict: refuted: resolve-out (else-branch does not satisfy postcondition, constraint #1)

name: table-frame
bug: also enters <ar$tpa, ar$tha> into the translation table, on the reasoning that a packet naming a target hardware address is free information; on a REPLY the target pair really is a valid binding, which is what makes the bug plausible, but the same code runs on a REQUEST where lines 184-185 say ar$tha was never set to anything in particular and line 186 offers the broadcast address as acceptable filler, so the step installs the target's protocol address bound to noise
shape: THE PRODUCT INVARIANT. LLMLL contracts are quantifier-free, so the frame condition is carried by a WITNESS KEY: `other` is a parameter constrained only to differ from the key the packet names, and because it is a parameter of a body-faithful function the solver proves the clause for all its values. This is the frame condition, not a sample of it
probe_verdict: SAFE (liquid-fixpoint), body_faithful true, display_level verified, one caller obligation (not (= other spa))
refuted_by: the two frame clauses, proved for all `other` and hence for the case other = tpa

name: spoof-binding
bug: MUTATION IS IN THE CONTRACT, NOT THE BODY, and this is the only probe where that is so. The mutant post claims the hardware address installed for <ar$pro, ar$spa> is the address that actually transmitted the frame. That is scope section 4's P-SPOOF and it is what most people believe ARP does. RFC 826's algorithm reads ar$sha out of the packet body, never compares it to the link-layer frame source, and performs the merge at lines 210-213 before the opcode is examined at line 219, so the claim is false of any faithful implementation
shape: the scope's intended NEGATIVE result, made mechanical. frame-src (S4) is in the signature and absent from the body, which is scope pre-commitment 4 (S4 is an observable, never a precondition on a transition) checkable by reading the body; the twin checks the other half, that the strengthened claim is refuted rather than quietly true
mutant_verdict: refuted: merge-binding (implementation does not satisfy postcondition, constraint #0)
refuted_by: the algorithm establishes no relation between ar$sha and the frame source, so no body implementing lines 203-225 can discharge the claim
